voice: James - Husky, Engaging and Bold (EkK5I93UQWFDigLMpZcX), eleven_v4

paras.text: [quietly] You're standing on the walls of Constantinople, the last city of the Roman Empire. It's the twenty-eighth of May, 1453.
Out in the dark is an army of maybe eighty thousand men. Every one of them serves a single family.
[measured] By tomorrow night, that family will have ended Rome.
A hundred and fifty years ago, they were a tribe on one hill, with land you could ride across in a day. All told, they'll rule for six hundred years.
Their story starts before Columbus is born. It ends when Americans are already driving Model Ts.
It nearly ended fifty years before tonight, when their sultan was taken prisoner and their empire was smashed to pieces. It came back. So what finally kills it?
[quietly] Two hundred and thirty years after tonight, this same army will be outside Vienna, with Europe counting the days it has left.
But to see how they got here, go back to around 1300, when the whole empire was this dot.

[measured] This is Anatolia, the big peninsula that's now most of Turkey. It's around 1300. The land is split into about twenty little Turkish states, each run by a chief called a bey. In time, one of them will swallow all the others.
They were the leftovers of a bigger Turkish kingdom that the Mongols had smashed.

Osman's piece was one of the smallest, a few hills around the town of Söğüt. Next door was the Byzantine Empire. That's the name historians give the eastern half of the Roman Empire, which had outlived the West by eight hundred years. Its people still called themselves Romans.
Later Ottoman storytellers said Osman once dreamed of a tree whose branches covered the world. Nobody wrote that down until a century after he died. The real Osman is almost a blank.

What we do know is where he stood. His border was his luck. It faced the richest Roman towns in Asia, close to Constantinople and badly defended. So fighters hungry for land, loot and holy war, called gazis, rode in from the other little states to join him.
Within a generation the war band had a capital, the old Roman city of Bursa, taken by Osman's son Orhan.

Then the Romans made what may have been the worst deal in their history. In the middle of a civil war, one side hired Orhan's soldiers to help it win. Its leader even gave Orhan his daughter as a wife.
The Romans had invited the Ottomans in. All the Ottomans needed now was a way across the water.

[measured] An earthquake in March 1354 knocked down the walls of Gallipoli, a Roman town on the European side of the strait. Orhan's eldest son was camped nearby with his men. They walked in, rebuilt the walls and refused to leave.

The Ottomans were in Europe now. They would stay for nearly six centuries. The next sultan, Murad, drove into the Balkans, the mountains of south-eastern Europe where Greeks, Bulgarians and Serbs lived, and moved his capital to the European side.
But conquered people make dangerous soldiers. Murad needed men who were loyal to him and to nobody else. [quietly] His answer ran on other people's sons.

[quietly] Picture a Christian village in the hills of Bosnia, a century or so later. An Ottoman officer arrives with a scribe. The village boys line up by the church. He picks the strongest and the sharpest, mostly teenagers. The scribe writes down each boy's name, his father and his village. The boys walk away with the officer, and most never come home.

This was the devşirme, which means "the collection". The boys were made Muslim, taught Turkish and trained. In law, they belonged to the sultan. Most became Janissaries, his own full-time foot soldiers, paid in cash and living in barracks.
The brightest went to a school inside the palace. One boy, taken from a Serbian family in Bosnia, grew up to run the whole empire as grand vizier, the sultan's chief minister.

How many boys were taken? Nobody knows. Every total we found fell apart the moment we looked for its source. To the families it was a tax paid in sons. To the sultan it was the perfect army: men with no family, no home town and nobody to be loyal to but him.

[measured] The family's second habit was darker. At Kosovo, in the Balkans, Murad's army met a Serbian-led army. Both leaders died that day. Murad's son Bayezid won the battle, then had his own brother killed on the spot, so nobody could ever challenge him.

Bayezid moved so fast they called him the Thunderbolt. He swallowed most of the other little Turkish states and wiped out an army of crusader knights from across Europe. For eight years he squeezed Constantinople, until people inside were running out of food.

But a bigger predator was coming from the east. Timur, a conqueror from Central Asia, had already carved out an empire from India to the Black Sea. Near Ankara, in the summer of 1402, he wiped out Bayezid's army and took the Thunderbolt prisoner. Within a year Bayezid was dead in captivity.
[somber] The sultan was gone. So was his army. Four of his sons were about to go to war over the pieces. Most empires never come back from a day like that.
[measured] For eleven years the brothers fought each other. One by one they died, until a single brother was left.

The empire lived through it because by now it could run for a while without a sultan. The Janissaries still drew their pay. The cavalry still got their land. Clerks kept the tax lists going. His son spent thirty years stitching the map back together.

Constantinople was a shell by then. It had once held maybe half a million people. Now fewer than fifty thousand lived among ruins and orchards inside walls built for a giant. Outside them, the Roman Empire was down to a few scraps of Greece.

In 1451 an eighteen-year-old named Mehmed became sultan. He wanted that city badly. It sat right between his European and Asian lands. Every ship going between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean had to sail past its walls.

A gun-maker named Orban, probably from Hungary, first offered his cannons to the Roman emperor. The emperor couldn't pay him. So Orban went to Mehmed, who could. His biggest gun was about eight metres long and fired stone balls that weighed hundreds of kilos.

The siege began in April. The land walls, a moat and two lines of stone, had stopped every army for a thousand years. Now the cannons hit them every day. Every night, the defenders filled the gaps with earth, timber and barrels.
A great iron chain blocked the city's harbour. So Mehmed had dozens of ships dragged over a hill on greased wooden tracks and dropped into the water behind it.

[quietly] A week before the end, the full moon rose dark, already in eclipse. To the people inside, it looked like a sign. On the last evening, the city crowded into its great church, Hagia Sophia, to pray. A few hours after midnight, the final attack began.

Mehmed sent his troops in waves. First came fighters he could afford to lose, then his regular army, then at first light the Janissaries. The Italian commander on the walls was badly wounded and carried away. The defence around him broke. Ottoman soldiers climbed the towers and raised their flags.
[somber] The last emperor was never seen alive again. Most accounts say he died fighting at the walls. The soldiers plundered the city. Thousands were killed. Thousands more were sold as slaves.
[quietly] A Greek writer who later worked for Mehmed says the sultan rode through the wrecked streets and cried out: "What a city we have given over to plunder and destruction!"

[measured] He rode on to Hagia Sophia and ordered it turned into a mosque. He made the city his capital and took a new title, Caesar of Rome. History calls him Mehmed the Conqueror. Remember the name Mehmed.
The Western half of Rome had fallen nearly a thousand years earlier. This was the end of the eastern half. The war band from one hill now held Rome's second capital.

[measured] Mehmed knew what four brothers at war had done to his family's empire. So he wrote the cure into law. Whichever son became sultan could put his brothers to death, "for the order of the world".
[quietly] The law got used. A century and a half later, one new sultan had all nineteen of his brothers strangled when he took the throne.
It was brutal. It also did what it was built to do. The empire never again broke into pieces the way it had after Timur.

The Conqueror's grandson Selim, remembered as Selim the Grim, ruled for only eight years and changed the shape of the map. He beat the new rulers of Persia, today's Iran. Then he turned south and destroyed the slave-soldier dynasty that ruled Egypt and Syria.

With Egypt came Cairo, Jerusalem and the protection of Islam's two holiest cities, Mecca and Medina. The empire grew by more than half. Its sultans now stood at the head of Sunni Islam, the biggest branch of the faith. In time they took the title of caliph, the leader of all Muslims.

Selim's son was Suleiman. Europeans called him the Magnificent. At Mohács in southern Hungary, his army destroyed the Hungarian army in about two hours. Hungary's young king drowned in a stream as he fled, leaving his kingdom in pieces.

Three years later he reached Vienna, capital of the Habsburgs, the family that led Catholic Europe. Rain had forced him to leave his biggest cannons behind. Winter was coming. After about three weeks, he turned back. It was the one great city he never took.
Everywhere else, he won. His empire ran from Algeria to Iraq and from Hungary to Yemen. Even the King of France was his ally against the Habsburgs.

[measured] Inside the palace, the danger was his own family. His wife Hürrem had been captured as a girl in what's now Ukraine and brought to the palace as a slave. He freed her and married her, which no sultan had done in generations.

[somber] His oldest living son wasn't hers. The soldiers loved that prince. Suleiman came to believe he was plotting to take the throne. So he called him into his tent and had him strangled. People at the time blamed Hürrem. Historians are less sure, and we think the rumour is too neat to trust.

Thirteen years later, Suleiman died in his own tent, during a siege in Hungary. His ministers hid his death from the army for weeks. If the soldiers had found out, they could have mutinied before the city fell.

[measured] In 1622, the sultan's own Janissaries stormed the palace. The sultan was seventeen and wanted to replace them with a new army. They dragged him to a fortress on the edge of the city and strangled him. No Ottoman sultan had ever been killed by his own people before.

The guards built to protect the family had learned they could kill it. By now they married, passed their places to their sons and rioted whenever their pay was late. And the princes were no longer killed. They were locked away in closed rooms inside the palace, sometimes for decades, and came out to rule knowing little of the world.

Still, the map held. Part of what held it together was the deal it offered the people it ruled. When Spain threw out its Jews in 1492, thousands sailed east. The sultan let them in. Salonica, a Greek port, became one of the biggest Jewish cities in the world.

If you were one of those families, you were safe. You also paid a tax your Muslim neighbour didn't. Your word counted for less in court. In many towns your church or synagogue couldn't stand taller than the mosque.
Safe, and second. Compared with what most of Europe offered people of the wrong faith, a lot of people took that deal.
[measured] Then the grand vizier, the sultan's chief minister, went after the one prize the empire had already missed. He marched on Vienna with one of the largest armies Europe had ever seen.
In the summer of 1683, the Ottoman army closes around the city.
Inside, the defenders have no hope of beating the army outside. They only have to last until help comes. And help is weeks away.
Ottoman miners dig tunnels under the walls, pack them with gunpowder and blow holes in them, again and again. Each time, the defenders plug the gap and fight in the rubble.
Every week there are fewer men left to do it. Early in September, the walls are breaking apart in places.
[quietly] Europe is counting the days it has left, and the count is almost done.
On the hills above the city, a relief army appears, led by the King of Poland.

After a day of fighting, about eighteen thousand horsemen, led by Poland's winged hussars, charge down the hills into the Ottoman camp. It's often called the largest cavalry charge in history. The Ottoman army breaks and runs.
[somber] On Christmas Day, on the sultan's orders, the grand vizier was strangled with a silk cord.

Austria, Poland, Venice and Russia smelled blood. They kept attacking for sixteen years. In the end, the Ottomans signed away most of Hungary. For almost four hundred years the map had mostly grown. From here on, it mostly shrank.

[measured] In 1826, the sultan turned his cannons on his own army. The Janissaries had blocked every reform for years. When they rose against him one more time, his new troops shelled their barracks. Thousands died. The corps that began with the stolen village boys was wiped out in a day.

It didn't look like strength from outside. A few decades later, Russia's tsar called the Ottoman Empire "a sick man, a very sick man". For a century, Western books told it as a story of endless decline. But a sick man doesn't usually take another seventy years to die.
Most historians who study the empire have dropped that decline story. We think they're right. The empire kept adapting. The trouble was that three enemies were closing in faster than it could change.

The first was money. Prices soared. The government cut the silver in its coins to pay its bills, so soldiers' wages melted away. Over the next two centuries, more and more of the world's trade moved to the Atlantic, where Europe's ocean empires were getting rich.
The second was a giant growing next door. Russia pushed south for two hundred years, until it took Crimea for itself.

The third was an idea. After the French Revolution, more and more people believed every nation should have its own country. The Serbs rose up, then the Greeks. Within one lifetime, Greece, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria had broken away.

The sultans raced to catch up. With the Janissaries gone, they built new schools, telegraph lines and railways. They promised equal treatment to every religion. They even gave the empire a constitution and a parliament.
They paid for it with borrowed money. About twenty years after the first foreign loan, the state couldn't pay its debts. European lenders moved in to collect several of its taxes themselves.

The next sultan shut parliament down and ruled alone for thirty years. [somber] Under his rule, in the 1890s, Armenians in the east were massacred. Historians' estimates of the dead run from about a hundred thousand to three hundred thousand.
[measured] The empire now had railways, newspapers and a modern army. That army's young officers had read about constitutions and nations. They were done waiting for the sultan.
Those officers, the Young Turks, forced the sultan to bring the constitution back in 1908. In the streets, Muslims, Christians and Jews celebrated together.
Within five years the celebrations were forgotten. Italy grabbed Libya. Two Balkan wars took almost all the empire's land in Europe. Three Young Turk leaders seized total power.

They took the empire into the First World War on Germany's side. A year later, British, French, Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Gallipoli, the same peninsula where the Ottomans had first stepped into Europe. After eight months of fighting, the invaders gave up and left. One of the Ottoman commanders who stopped them was Mustafa Kemal.

[somber] In the same year, the government turned on its own Armenian citizens, a Christian people who had lived in Anatolia for more than two thousand years. Some two hundred and fifty Armenian community leaders in Istanbul were arrested, and most were later killed.

[somber] Then Armenians across Anatolia were forced from their homes. Many of the men were shot. Women, children and the old were marched toward the Syrian desert, where huge numbers died of hunger, disease and massacre.

[quietly] Historians' estimates of the dead run from about six hundred thousand to more than a million. Armenia puts it at one and a half million. Most historians call it genocide, and so do the United States and more than thirty other countries. Turkey accepts that many Armenians died, but rejects the word genocide and says the deaths were part of a wartime collapse in which many Muslims died too. Assyrians and Greeks were also killed in these years.

The empire lost the war. British armies took Baghdad and Jerusalem while Arab forces rose against the sultan. By the autumn of 1918, the empire had surrendered. British and French troops marched into Istanbul. Two years later the winners handed the sultan a treaty that carved up even the Turkish heartland, and his government signed it.
[measured] Mustafa Kemal refused to accept it. From Ankara he raised a new army and a new government. Then he won a war of independence against the invaders. After that, he turned to the sultan.

His parliament in Ankara abolished the sultanate in November 1922. Two weeks later, the last sultan, Mehmed the Sixth, slipped out of his palace under British protection and boarded a British battleship, HMS Malaya.
[quietly] Four hundred and sixty-nine years earlier, Mehmed the Conqueror had ridden into this city and called himself Caesar of Rome. Now another Mehmed was sailing out of it on a foreign warship.

[measured] So that's what finally killed it. Timur couldn't do it. Neither could Vienna, or two hundred years of shrinking. It took one of its own officers, the hero of Gallipoli, deciding the Turks would do better without a sultan at all. Within two years there was a republic, and no caliph either.
But the family still didn't die. Every member was sent into exile in 1924. The men weren't allowed back into Turkey for half a century.
The House of Osman still has a head today. He's a great-grandson of the sultan who ruled alone, born in exile in 1932.
[quietly] Six hundred years after a tribe on one hill, the family is still here. The Rome they finished off is not. The story of that Rome, from its very first day, starts here.
